meta.title: PyRIT · agent targets
meta.subtitle: the pitch in visual form · drafts #15–#25 on spencrr/PyRIT
meta.version: deck v2 · fork spencrr/PyRIT · base microsoft/PyRIT 6a2319644

glossary.ACP: Agent Client Protocol: JSON-RPC over stdio between a client (here PyRIT) and an agent harness. The same protocol editors use to drive coding agents.
glossary.harness: The agent program under test (Copilot CLI, an Agent Framework host, any ACP agent): it plans, calls tools and talks to a model.
glossary.journal: PyRIT's append-only record of every ACP frame, lifecycle event and inference call for one execution (events.jsonl). Redacted before writing.
glossary.lease: An execution-scoped credential for the inference relay: a bearer token with a call budget, revoked when the execution closes.
glossary.projection: The rule that turns journaled tool_call frames into function_call / function_call_output memory pieces, or omits them with a reason.
glossary.relay: PyRIT's local OpenAI-compatible endpoint that validates each harness request against the bound target and forwards it with the single-inference capability.
glossary.provider: An ExecutionEnvironmentProvider: code that allocates, launches and releases the place a harness runs (local, docker, yours).
glossary.adapter: A HarnessAdapter: how one kind of harness is launched and pointed at a model.
glossary.execution: One owned, stateful instance: one native agent session in one environment, created on a conversation's first message and reused for later turns.
glossary.recipe: Model binding + harness profile + environment template + policy: the configuration whose hash is the target's identity.
glossary.seam: A contract between PyRIT core and extension code, verified by an executable conformance suite.
glossary.conformance: A suite that drives a real provider or adapter through its contract and reports one check per promise.
glossary.Co-PyRIT: PyRIT's web UI and REST API.
glossary.piece: A MessagePiece in PyRIT memory: text, function_call, function_call_output and other typed content scorers read.
glossary.BYOM: Bring your own model: bind a registered PyRIT target behind the harness so the model and the harness are testable independently.

steps.eyebrow: PyRIT · agents as targets · the pitch, the map, three perspectives
steps.lede: PyRIT can red-team an **agent**, not just a model: a harness that plans, calls tools and changes state inside an environment PyRIT owns and disposes of. Everything is swappable; everything is recorded; a person can say no.

steps.title: What you will see
steps.lede: The **tour** (≈6 min) is the pitch in visual form: a cold open, four claims, a recipe you can swap live, the map, and a day in the life of an operator, an administrator and an extender. The **deep dive** adds the mechanism chapters with pinned code. Press `T` any time to switch.

principles.title: Agents are targets
principles.text: Attacks, converters and scorers do not know an agent is on the other side.

principles.title: Everything is swappable

chapters.title: What just happened
chapters.summary: A one-line request, a real agent that reads a file and writes a receipt, and a scorer that reads what it did.
chapters.takeaway: PyRIT just red-teamed an **agent**: not a model's text, but a program that acted.

legend.label: The agent and what it touched

steps.title: “Create the receipt.”
steps.body: One ordinary PyRIT message. Nothing in the attack, the converters or the scorers knows that the thing on the other side is an agent.

captions.label: fixture
captions.text: Everything in this chapter is a real capture from the scripted ACP agent in the repository.

steps.title: The agent plans, reads a file, does arithmetic
steps.body: It calls `read_orders({"path": "orders.json"})`, gets the items back, and answers “Receipt total: 31”. That is behaviour, not prose: a tool call with a result, inside a workspace PyRIT gave it.

slots.agent.plan: read the order, then write the receipt

captions.label: the agent
captions.text: A harness such as GitHub Copilot CLI, speaking the Agent Client Protocol over stdio.

steps.title: A scorer reads what it did, not only what it said
steps.body: The tool call and its result arrive in PyRIT memory as the same `function_call` / `function_call_output` pieces existing tool-call scorers already read, each pointing back to the exact journal frame it came from.

slots.scorer.verdict: did it act as instructed? yes

captions.label: five ways
captions.text: That one `{"total": 31}` appears as a wire frame, a journal line, a memory piece, an operator's approval and a score. Keep an eye on it.

chapters.title: PyRIT can red-team an agent, not just a model
chapters.summary: Four claims and one thing that does not change.
chapters.takeaway: The thing under test is a **harness** that plans, calls tools and changes state inside an environment PyRIT owns and disposes of.

actors.label: Agents are targets
actors.sub: `AgentTarget` is one more `PromptTarget`. Attacks, converters and scorers run against it **unchanged**.

actors.label: Did, not said
actors.sub: PyRIT records every protocol frame and projects the agent's **actions** into memory as tool-call pieces.

actors.label: Bring your own model
actors.sub: The model behind the agent can be a **PyRIT target** behind a scoped relay; the harness and the model become independently testable.

actors.label: People in the loop
actors.sub: Operators watch live, approve or deny tool permissions, hold, cancel and close; decisions are attributed.

steps.title: Four claims, each verifiable end to end
steps.body: This is the whole pitch. Each claim maps to a chapter of this tour and to one or two pull requests in the stack; nothing here is aspirational.

slots.c1.so: your existing test suite runs against agents
slots.c2.so: scores are about behaviour, with provenance
slots.c3.so: swap the model, hold the harness (or vice versa)
slots.c4.so: a human can say no, mid-run

captions.label: source
captions.text: The one-sentence pitch in the design gist, split into its four load-bearing parts.

steps.title: Everything above the target is untouched
steps.body: No new attack types, no new scorer types, no new memory schema. The agent arrives as a target; what it did arrives as pieces. That is why the stack can start with two small core PRs and why the rest is reviewable brick by brick.

captions.label: one new seam in core
captions.text: Targets gained an explicit **outcome** (PR 1) and a **single-inference** capability (PR 3); both are useful without agents.

chapters.title: A target is a recipe
chapters.summary: Swap the model, the harness, the environment or the policy and watch the identity change; change a timeout and watch it not.
chapters.takeaway: Model binding + harness profile + environment template + policy → a configured target that **owns no resources**. Identity is the hash of the recipe; preset names are provenance.

recipe.note: Illustration of the rule in `AgentTarget._build_identifier` (configuration without defaults, timeouts and budgets); the bytes PyRIT hashes are pydantic's serialization, so the digits differ.

options.label: harness default
options.desc: The harness authenticates itself (e.g. `COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN`); PyRIT records that no binding exists.

options.label: openai_chat
options.desc: A registered `OpenAIChatTarget` answers every completion through the relay.

options.label: ollama_local
options.desc: A local model behind the same relay; the harness cannot tell the difference.

options.label: agent_framework
options.desc: PyRIT's ACP host running a Microsoft Agent Framework agent.

options.label: any ACP agent
options.desc: The scripted agent used for this deck's fixtures, or your own.

options.label: docker
options.desc: Container per execution, labelled and capability-dropped; the reference isolated provider.

options.label: local
options.desc: A subprocess with a private home. **Not** a sandbox; requires an explicit acknowledgement.

options.label: aca-sandbox
options.desc: An out-of-tree cloud provider built against the same contract.

options.label: deny
options.desc: Default. Every tool permission request is refused; the agent is told so.

options.label: allow_once
options.desc: Each request is granted once, deterministically.

options.label: ask
options.desc: An operator decides in Co-PyRIT; only valid for interactive sends.

excluded.label: Timeouts · budgets
excluded.desc: Turn deadline, idle expiry, lifetime, evidence and artifact budgets: execution policy, **excluded** from identity.

steps.title: Four parts you can swap
steps.body: Which model answers, which agent runs and how it is launched, where it runs, and what happens when it asks for permission. Each part is reusable and registered by setup. Use the arrows to swap any of them.

captions.label: try it
captions.text: ‹ › on any card; the hash below updates live.

captions.label: presets
captions.text: Preset names are kept as provenance, never hashed.

steps.title: Swap the model: a different system under test
steps.body: Bind `openai_chat`. The harness is identical, but the recipe changed, so the identity changed: results from this target never mix with the previous one. This is **bring your own model**: the harness will reach the bound target only through PyRIT's relay.

captions.label: why it matters
captions.text: Regressions can be attributed to the model or to the scaffolding, not to “the agent”.

focus: Timeouts and evidence budgets are execution policy

steps.title: Swap where it runs
steps.body: Same model, same harness, now in a local process instead of a container. `environment` has no default: a target must say where it runs, and a non-isolated provider must be acknowledged.

captions.label: providers
captions.text: `local` and `docker` ship with PyRIT; an ACA sandbox provider was built out of tree against the same contract.

evidence.title: A template is never a live resource

steps.title: Permission policy is identity, and it defaults to deny
steps.body: A target that **asks an operator** and one that **denies** every tool permission are different systems under test, so the policy is hashed. New targets refuse permission requests unless you say otherwise; `ask` is only valid for interactive chat and fails fast for attacks.

captions.label: not enforcement
captions.text: The policy is a deterministic protocol answer; isolation comes from the environment.

steps.title: Tighten a deadline: same identity
steps.body: Timeouts, holds, evidence and artifact budgets are **execution policy**. Change them and the hash is unchanged: results stay comparable across a deadline tweak, while changing what runs or where creates a new target.

captions.label: rule
captions.text: `exclude_defaults=True, exclude=_IDENTITY_EXCLUDED_FIELDS` on the configuration dump.

steps.title: Hold one, swap the other
steps.body: Two harnesses × two models = four systems under test, each with its own identity and its own results. Is the regression in the model or in the scaffolding? Run the row, run the column.

captions.label: in practice
captions.text: Compose each cell from the same presets in YAML; names are provenance, so the matrix is auditable.

focus: Origin retained outside the target's identity

chapters.title: Core owns policy, extensions own resources
chapters.summary: The components, who owns what, and the two seams a reviewer should hold in mind.
chapters.takeaway: Everything PyRIT-owned sits in **core** and runs once; everything that allocates or runs sits behind a **seam** PyRIT can verify.

steps.title: Nothing above the target changes
steps.body: Attacks send messages; converters rewrite them; scorers read the pieces that come back; memory stores them. An agent target sits where any target sits. Operators and administrators meet the system in Co-PyRIT.

captions.label: reading the map
captions.text: Left to right: who asks → what owns the policy → who owns the resources.

steps.title: Core: the policy, implemented once
steps.body: The execution manager owns timeouts, budgets, cancellation and reconciliation. The journal records every frame. The projection turns frames into pieces. Approvals route permission requests to policy or a person. The relay stands between the harness and any model. The ACP client speaks the protocol.

captions.label: why once
captions.text: A provider cannot weaken redaction or budgets by accident, because it never sees them.

steps.title: Two seams, both executable
steps.body: `HarnessAdapter`: how a kind of harness is launched and pointed at a model. `ExecutionEnvironmentProvider`: four moments (reserve, translate the relay URL, launch, close). Each has a conformance suite that drives a real implementation and reports one check per promise.

captions.label: for reviewers
captions.text: A provider PR is reviewed against its conformance report, not against a reading of the ABC.

steps.title: Extensions own what gets allocated
steps.body: An environment (local process, Docker container, your sandbox) that contains the harness process and a workspace seeded from the template. The harness reaches a model only through the relay, with a lease, so no provider credential ever enters the environment.

captions.label: disposed
captions.text: Closing an execution releases exactly what the provider allocated, and refuses anything it did not create.

steps.title: The same map, as the reviewers see it
steps.takeaway: The runtime-architecture diagram from the design gist. Everything on this tour is a zoom into one of its regions; the minimap in the header shows which.
steps.note: SVG source and PNG on the `agents/stack-assets` branch; the gist embeds the same image.

chapters.title: Ask, watch, approve
chapters.summary: A Co-PyRIT chat replayed from a real journal: send, watch the agent act, decide a permission, read the score.
chapters.takeaway: Operators see **what the agent does**, live, and can **say no** mid-run. Every decision is attributed and journaled.

steps.title: Pick an agent target like any other
steps.body: In Co-PyRIT chat the target picker lists `receipt_agent` next to every other registered target. Model, harness profile and environment template are fixed for the conversation; a status strip shows the feed, the ACP connection and the environment.

captions.label: fixture
captions.text: This replay is driven by `ask_events.jsonl`, a real journal captured with `permission_policy=ask`.

captions.label: mock
captions.text: The chat is a faithful mock; the real screenshots follow.

steps.title: The first message provisions an execution
steps.body: `initialize`, `session/new`, then `session/prompt`. The environment is allocated, the harness launched and connected; from now on the conversation reuses this execution. The journal on the right is the same data the chat streams over SSE.

captions.label: status strip
captions.text: Feed: live · ACP: ready · Environment: local / working · Cancel turn · Close execution.

steps.title: Watch it act
steps.body: “I will read the order.” Then a `tool_call` named `read_orders`. The activity panel renders each streamed update under the message as it arrives; nothing is invented from the agent's prose.

captions.label: did, not said
captions.text: Only explicit, named tool calls with established results become memory pieces.

steps.title: The agent asks; the execution is held
steps.body: `session/request_permission` for “Read orders.json”. With the `ask` policy the runtime turns it into an approval and holds the execution: **Allow once** or **Deny** appear under the tool call, with the deadline. The harness had to offer a `reject_once` option, so a denial can be expressed as a denial.

captions.label: try it
captions.text: Click **Allow once** in the mock.

captions.label: attacks
captions.text: Automated attacks cannot use `ask`; they fail fast instead of hanging.

steps.title: An operator allows it, once
steps.body: `permission.resolved · operator_allow` names the operator. The reply goes back to the agent as the `allow_once` option it offered, the tool runs, and `tool_call_update` carries the real result. Decisions are server-owned, so a refresh or a second tab cannot lose or double-answer one.

captions.label: attribution
captions.text: Visible to everyone with access to the attack by default; `show_agent_operator_identity: false` shows roles instead.

steps.title: “Receipt total: 31”, and a score about what it did
steps.body: The turn completes. The transcript stores the assistant text plus the projected tool pieces; Co-PyRIT auto-scores completed assistant and tool pieces with whatever scorer you configured. The agent's words and its actions are both evidence now.

captions.label: outcome
captions.text: A turn with tool effects and no text would still be `completed`, which is why PR 1 made outcomes explicit.

steps.title: The second message reuses the execution
steps.body: “Add one orange to the order” changes a file the agent itself wrote earlier: the total goes from 31 to 36. Same execution, same workspace, same journal; a stateful system under test, not a stateless endpoint.

captions.label: lifetime
captions.text: The execution ends on explicit close, idle expiry, its maximum lifetime, a turn deadline, or runtime shutdown.

steps.title: It is real: the permission moment
steps.takeaway: The same flow in the actual Co-PyRIT UI, captured headlessly against this branch with the scripted agent and the local provider. Status strip, activity, the pending approval with **Allow once / Deny**, and the deadline.
steps.note: `fixtures/real/capture.mjs` reproduces this capture; no credentials involved.
steps.alt: Co-PyRIT chat with a pending tool permission

steps.title: It is real: two turns later
steps.takeaway: Second turn complete: `Receipt total: 36`, the stored tool-call pieces (“journal event 22 · 23”), and the honest footnote: *exposed ACP events retained; missing tool calls are undetermined, not false*.
steps.note: The footnote is the projection's contract in one sentence.
steps.alt: Co-PyRIT chat after the second turn

chapters.title: Create, gate, govern, clean up
chapters.summary: Who may create agent targets, what the defaults are, how executions are listed and closed, and what the catalog reveals.
chapters.takeaway: Every execution launches a process with credentials the server holds. Creation is **admin-only**, defaults are **safe**, resources are **visible and closable**.

steps.title: One form, three sections, in that order
steps.body: *Model* picks a registered connection for BYOM or lets the harness authenticate itself. *Harness* and *Environment* offer registered presets; choosing one locks its fields and records the names as provenance, *Customize* copies the values and drops the provenance. Nothing in the form ever resolves a credential: credential fields hold variable **names**.

captions.label: real screenshot
captions.text: Next step shows the actual form.

steps.title: The real form
steps.takeaway: Captured from this branch: Model · Harness · Environment, *Ask me* selected for the demo, *Local process* with the acknowledgement that local tools can access the host.
steps.note: Preset dropdowns are empty here because the demo backend registers no presets; with initializers they list named profiles and templates.
steps.alt: Create New Target form for Agent (ACP)

steps.title: Admin-only, one validated object, confined fixtures
steps.body: `requires_admin_creation` is a class marker checked by the create-target service next to upstream's `code_execution_parameter` and `server_credential_parameter`. `agent_configuration` crosses REST as one JSON object because the model opts in with `JsonParameterValue`; exactly one parameter in the repository does. A fixture directory must resolve inside the server's `target_upload_directory`.

captions.label: why
captions.text: Every execution launches a process or container with credentials the server holds, regardless of parameters.

steps.title: Deny by default; local must be acknowledged
steps.body: New targets, in Python and in the UI, refuse tool permission requests. `allow_once` and `ask` are explicit choices; `ask` is only valid for interactive chat sends and fails fast for attacks. Choosing a provider that is not isolated requires ticking *I understand local tools can access the host*.

captions.label: identity
captions.text: Policy is part of the target's identity: deny-targets and ask-targets never share results.

steps.title: Executions are resources: listed, closable, reconciled
steps.body: `Registry → Agent executions` lists what the backend owns with its state (`starting · idle · working · held · closing · closed · cleanup_failed`), its profile and environment, and the last turn. Administrators can cancel a turn or close an execution, including retrying failed cleanup. Interrupted executions are reconciled on restart through the same provider path.

slots.registry.state: starting · idle · working · held · closing · closed · cleanup_failed

captions.label: observation
captions.text: Watching an execution never renews its lifetime; only work does.

steps.title: The real registry
steps.takeaway: Captured after the chat above: the `receipt_agent` execution idle on `local` with its last turn completed, next to an older, closed one. This is the administrator's resource view, separate from the chat.
steps.note: Observation does not renew expiry; the idle execution closes on its idle timeout or when an administrator closes it.

steps.title: Three knobs worth knowing
steps.body: `show_agent_operator_identity` (default **show**) controls whether decisions name the operator or just the role. Per-execution inference budgets default to 100 requests and cap at 1,000. Live executions, including idle and held chats, block configuration replacement exactly as active sends and scenario runs do.

slots.settings.replace: blocked while any execution is live

captions.label: presentation only
captions.text: Masking identity changes nothing stored; the record and the admin view keep it.

steps.title: What everyone can see, and what no one can
steps.body: The target catalog shows credential variable **names** and the resolved fixture path to every authenticated user: that is the authoring contract. Values never appear anywhere: not in the catalog, not in the journal (redacted before writing), not in conversation routes (which omit owner, provider and process identities).

slots.catalog.names: credential variable names · fixture path · presets
slots.catalog.never: credential values · image digest · process identities (conversation routes)

captions.label: declined review item
captions.text: Hiding the names was considered and declined: operators need to know which variables a profile expects.

chapters.title: Make PyRIT use my sandbox
chapters.summary: Implement four moments, run the conformance suite, register through setup; the same for a new harness.
chapters.takeaway: PyRIT does not own environments or harnesses. It owns the **contract** and the **suite that checks it**; an out-of-tree provider needed zero core changes.

moments.title: reserve()
moments.text: Record deterministic resource identifiers before anything exists, so a crash mid-allocation stays reconcilable.

moments.title: inference_endpoint_async(relay_url)
moments.text: Translate the relay URL into your network namespace. Must not acquire resources.

moments.title: launch_async(spec)
moments.text: Seed the workspace, acquire resources, start the harness. Only variable names on command lines; values through your own channel.

moments.title: close_async()
moments.text: Release exactly what you own, collect artifacts, stay idempotent, refuse anything you did not create.

steps.title: Four moments, two byte streams
steps.body: A provider subclasses `ExecutionEnvironmentProvider` (an `info` description, template validation, `create_session`) and returns an `ExecutionSession` with four lifecycle methods and three streams: ACP reader, ACP writer, stderr. Nothing here speaks ACP; you move bytes and honour the moments.

captions.label: policy stays in core
captions.text: Timeouts, budgets, redaction and the protocol are not yours to implement, or to weaken.

steps.title: Run the conformance suite against a real allocation
steps.body: `verify_environment_provider_async` drives one real allocation with a byte-echo command and reports one check per promise: streams unavailable before launch, relay translation, a secret that must not leak, idempotent release, honest capabilities. This report is the real one for the `local` provider, captured while building this deck: 17 of 17.

captions.label: review
captions.text: A provider PR is reviewed against this report; Docker's runs in integration tests.

steps.title: Register through setup, never from the UI
steps.body: Providers and adapters are trusted code registered by setup (`EnvironmentProviderRegistry.register`), not import strings accepted over REST. Templates then name your provider by its `info.name`, and the UI lists the template fields your provider declares.

captions.label: ACA
captions.text: The Azure Container Apps sandbox provider was built this way outside the repository with zero core changes; packaging waits on the preview CLI.

steps.title: A new harness is an adapter, not a fork
steps.body: `HarnessAdapter` declares `info` (name, default command, wire APIs, native credential names, reserved variables), `launch_environment` (how the harness finds its private home) and `inference_environment` (how it is pointed at the relay). `verify_harness_adapter` checks those promises without running anything. Copilot CLI and the Agent Framework host are the two shipped adapters; a generic ACP adapter covers the rest.

captions.label: reserved
captions.text: Process identity and lookup paths (HOME, PATH, …) can never be credential references.

steps.title: Known limits
steps.takeaway: Said plainly, so reviewers do not have to find them.

bullets.title: Budgets are per execution
bullets.text: Default 100 inference requests, max 1,000; per-turn budgets are deferred.

bullets.title: Modality is declared, not policed per request
bullets.text: The binding declares input modalities; undeclared image parts are not yet rejected by the relay.

bullets.title: `local` is not a sandbox
bullets.text: Private home and workspace only; it requires an explicit acknowledgement.

bullets.title: Permission policy is not enforcement
bullets.text: It is a deterministic ACP answer; isolation comes from the environment.

bullets.title: Tool coverage is what the protocol exposes
bullets.text: Missing tool calls are undetermined, not false; the UI says so under every turn.

steps.title: Deferred on purpose
steps.takeaway: Each has a place in the stack where it would land; none is needed to test an agent today.

bullets.title: Agent configuration registry UI · create by preset name
bullets.text: After 6b. Does **not** replace the three-panel form.

bullets.title: Checkpoint save / restore
bullets.text: After 2b, as an optional Docker-provider capability.

bullets.title: Durable startup authoring · evidence playback
bullets.text: After 5 / after 6a. “Download journal” covers today's need.

bullets.title: Managed cloud providers (ACA)
bullets.text: Proven out of tree; packaging waits on the preview CLI/SDK.

chapters.title: Eleven claims, one linear chain
chapters.summary: Hover a PR to read its claim, why it is separate, and what it needs. Dashed nodes are deferred on purpose.

steps.title: Eleven claims, one linear chain

nodes.title: Explicit target outcomes
nodes.claim: A target can complete without assistant text. Every `TargetResponse` declares an explicit outcome instead of letting an empty string mean anything.
facts: Core-model change touching every target; approved on its own merits.

nodes.title: Single-inference capability
nodes.claim: Targets expose a single-inference capability: transport and auth without history or a tool loop. Independent of 1; the relay (4) is its first consumer.
facts: General target capability owned by target maintainers; sequencing-free.

nodes.label: 2a
nodes.title: ACP runtime + environment seam
nodes.claim: Existing attacks run against an ACP agent in an owned execution; the environment is a provider contract PyRIT verifies with an executable conformance suite.
facts: `AgentTarget`, `AgentExecutionManager`, journal, `local` provider, Copilot + generic adapters, `requires_admin_creation`, `JsonParameterValue` opt-in, conformance suites
policy in core; nothing provider-specific leaks in

nodes.label: ext
nodes.title: ACA sandbox provider
nodes.claim: Built against the 2a contract outside the repository with zero core changes; packaging waits on the preview CLI/SDK.

nodes.label: 2b
nodes.title: Docker reference provider
nodes.claim: Docker is the reference isolated provider others base theirs on: labels, capability drops, limits, image provenance, ownership-checked teardown.
facts: PyRIT does not own environments; this is the worked example.

nodes.label: 2c
nodes.title: Tool calls as pieces
nodes.claim: What the agent did lands as `function_call` / `function_call_output` pieces PyRIT's tool-call scorers already read, with provenance and explicit omissions.
facts: Faithfulness of tool records is the false-evidence review; it deserves undivided attention.

nodes.label: later
nodes.title: Checkpoint save / restore
nodes.claim: Re-lands as an optional Docker-provider capability once the base provider is reviewed.

nodes.title: Target-backed model (BYOK)
nodes.claim: The model behind the agent is a PyRIT target: relay, lease, binding and parameter-conflict rules. A distinct trust boundary.
facts: Scoped authority; the credential never leaves the server.

nodes.title: Reusable configuration
nodes.claim: Agents compose from initializers and registries; names are provenance, not identity.
facts: Config-plane change: YAML contract and provenance.

nodes.title: Agent Framework ACP host
nodes.claim: Host Microsoft Agent Framework agents over ACP as an optional extra; doubles as the login-free CI proof of the full ACP path.
facts: 7, so the fork shows one linear chain

nodes.label: later
nodes.title: Relay modality · turn budgets
nodes.claim: Per-request modality enforcement and per-turn inference budgets change evidence semantics; deferred with the limits documented in chapter 04.

nodes.label: later
nodes.title: Durable startup authoring
nodes.claim: Persisting a reproducible definition is independent of basic agent testing.

nodes.label: 6a
nodes.title: Co-PyRIT API
nodes.claim: Create agent targets, send, stream activity, inspect executions: curl-verifiable without the UI.

nodes.label: later
nodes.title: Evidence packages / playback
nodes.claim: “Download journal” covers the need; playback is its own UX.

nodes.label: 6b
nodes.title: Co-PyRIT UI
nodes.claim: Configure agents (three-panel Create Target form) and watch what they do, integrated with the hook-based ChatWindow.

nodes.title: Interactive controls
nodes.claim: Operators approve, cancel and hold; a control-plane change separate from observation.

nodes.label: later
nodes.title: Agent config registry UI
nodes.claim: A Registry tab to browse presets and an optional “create by preset name” path. Does **not** replace the three-panel form.

steps.footer: **Promotion.** #15 and #16 are independent and go first; each later PR is rebased onto `main` once its predecessor merges. Base: upstream `microsoft/PyRIT` main at `6a2319644`. The unsliced proof of concept lives on `agents/integration` (reference only). Story gist: gist.github.com/spencrr/474c66a5f7c569106b5068b7477d4e90

steps.title: How to review
steps.takeaway: Each PR carries its feature commit plus the fixes from two skeptical reviews as separate `FIX`/`TEST` commits, so you can see what the review changed. Each PR body lists the exact commands run and their results.

chapters.eyebrow: Deep dive 11 · one turn, end to end
chapters.title: One turn, end to end
chapters.summary: An attack sends one message; a real agent plans, calls a tool, answers; PyRIT returns what it did.
chapters.takeaway: The thing under test is a **harness** that plans, calls tools and changes state inside an environment PyRIT owns. Existing attacks, scorers and converters run against it **unchanged**.

legend.label: Agent-owned · harness, its frames, its effects

steps.title: One turn, end to end
steps.takeaway: Follow a single message from an unchanged attack through a real agent and back. Everything on this stage is either **PyRIT-owned** (mint) or **agent-owned** (amber); the border between them is the point of the design.

steps.title: The attack does not know it is talking to an agent
steps.body: `AgentTarget` is one more `PromptTarget`. It accepts the current user message only and **never replays tool-producing history** to the harness: the agent owns its own session state.

captions.label: attack
captions.text: Any existing attack, converter chain or scorer.

captions.label: target
captions.text: Validates user text; hands the message to the execution manager.

steps.title: First message: an execution is allocated and launched
steps.body: The manager persists a record, asks the **environment provider** for a session, reserves deterministic resource identifiers, then launches the harness command with a private home. State moves `starting → idle`. Every later message in this conversation reuses the same execution.

captions.label: runtime
captions.text: `record.json` is written before any resource exists, so a crash is reconcilable.

captions.label: environment
captions.text: `reserve` → `inference_endpoint_async` → `launch_async`; the provider owns the resources.

steps.title: Every ACP frame is journaled before it is sent or acted on
steps.body: `session/prompt` goes out; the harness streams `session/update` notifications back: a `tool_call`, its `tool_call_update` with the result, an `agent_message_chunk`. The transport records **intent before writing** and retains every valid incoming frame, including extensions it does not understand.

captions.label: harness
captions.text: Plans, calls its tool, streams what it is doing. PyRIT does not interpret, it records.

captions.label: journal
captions.text: Append-only `events.jsonl`; the flushed journal is the commit point.

steps.title: The model behind the agent is a PyRIT target
steps.body: When the harness wants a completion it calls what it believes is an OpenAI endpoint. That endpoint is PyRIT's **inference relay**: an execution-scoped bearer lease, a per-execution call budget, and a forward to whichever registered PyRIT target the operator bound. The provider credential never enters the environment.

captions.label: harness → relay
captions.text: `POST /v1/chat/completions` with the execution token. Path, model and body shape are policed.

captions.label: relay → target
captions.text: Single-inference capability of the bound target: transport + auth, no history, no tool loop.

evidence.title: Binding a lease to an execution

steps.limit: Budgets are per execution lifetime (default 100, max 1,000); per-turn accounting is deferred.

steps.title: What the agent did becomes pieces PyRIT already understands
steps.body: The turn finishes. From the journaled frames of this turn, `project_agent_tools` emits `function_call` / `function_call_output` pieces, each carrying provenance back to the exact event sequence. Nothing is inferred from the agent's prose.

captions.label: projection
captions.text: Explicit name, object arguments, granted permission, established result; otherwise omitted **with a reason**.

captions.label: memory
captions.text: Same piece types `MessageToolCallScorer` reads today.

steps.title: An explicit outcome, not an empty string
steps.body: `TargetResponse` carries `outcome=completed` plus execution and turn identifiers in metadata. A turn that produced tool effects but no assistant text is still a **completed** turn, which is why the stack starts with explicit target outcomes (PR 1).

captions.label: outcome
captions.text: `completed` · `refused` · `failed` … every target declares one; agents just made it unavoidable.

captions.label: scoring
captions.text: Only completed assistant/tool pieces are auto-scored in Co-PyRIT.

chapters.title: Core owns policy, providers own resources
chapters.summary: Two executable contracts separate PyRIT's runtime from wherever the agent runs: local, Docker, or your own sandbox.
chapters.takeaway: PyRIT does **not** own environments. It owns **policy**: timeouts, budgets, cancellation, approvals, redaction and the ACP protocol. A provider owns **resources**: allocation, release, workspace seeding and the byte streams. The seam between them is a contract PyRIT can verify.

actors.label: Providers · resources
actors.tag: registered by setup, never from the UI

actors.label: ACA sandbox
actors.sub: modelled on the Docker provider · zero core changes

actors.label: your provider
actors.sub: any place that can move bytes and honour four moments

steps.title: The environment seam
steps.takeaway: Where the agent runs is a **provider decision**. Which rules apply is a **PyRIT decision**. Chapter 02 walks the contract between them and the three providers that exercise it: `local`, `docker`, and an out-of-tree cloud sandbox.

steps.title: Everything that is policy lives in core, once
steps.body: Timeouts, inference budgets, cancellation grace, permission policy, credential redaction and the ACP client are implemented exactly once, in `pyrit.agent`. A provider cannot weaken them, because it never sees them.

captions.label: core
captions.text: Trusted code that ships with PyRIT.

captions.label: why
captions.text: A sandbox vendor should not be able to turn off redaction by accident.

steps.title: A provider owns exactly four moments
steps.body: `reserve` records deterministic resource identifiers before anything exists, so a crash mid-allocation is reconcilable. `inference_endpoint_async` translates the relay URL into the environment's network namespace **without acquiring resources**. `launch_async` seeds the workspace and starts the harness. `close_async` releases only what it owns and is idempotent.

captions.label: streams
captions.text: `acp_reader`, `acp_writer`, `stderr` raise `RuntimeError` before a successful launch.

captions.label: secrets
captions.text: Only variable **names** travel on command lines; values travel through the provider's own channel.

steps.title: `local`: the smallest honest provider
steps.body: A subprocess with a fresh empty workspace and a private home, running as the backend's own OS user. It is **not** a sandbox and says so: creating a local target requires an explicit acknowledgement. It is what development and CI use, and it proves the seam needs no container to be meaningful.

captions.label: local
captions.text: `LocalSession(SubprocessSession)`; stop the owned process tree, keep requested artifacts, remove runtime directories.

steps.title: `docker`: the reference isolated provider
steps.body: One container per execution, labelled with the execution and owner identifiers. Capabilities dropped, `no-new-privileges`, a pid limit, memory and CPU limits, and the network the template chose. Only variable names appear on the `docker create` command line; values travel through the docker CLI's own environment.

captions.label: provenance
captions.text: The resolved image id is recorded on the execution, not just the tag.

captions.label: template
captions.text: `EnvironmentTemplate` is a reusable starting filesystem and access policy, never a running environment.

steps.title: Teardown refuses anything it did not create
steps.body: Before stopping a container, the provider inspects it and compares the `pyrit.execution` and `pyrit.owner` labels with the record. A name collision with someone else's container is an error, not a cleanup.

captions.label: interrupted runs
captions.text: On restart, `_reconcile_interrupted_async` recreates the session from the record and releases it through the same path.

steps.title: The contract is executable
steps.body: `verify_environment_provider_async` drives one real allocation through the provider with a byte-echo command and reports one check per promise: streams unavailable before launch, relay translation, a secret that must not leak, idempotent release, honest capabilities. The ACA sandbox provider was built against this suite **outside the repository with zero core changes**.

captions.label: for maintainers
captions.text: A provider PR is reviewed against the report, not against a reading of the ABC.

captions.label: for vendors
captions.text: Nothing here speaks ACP; a provider only has to move bytes and honour the four moments.

steps.review: Review a provider by running its conformance report in CI; the Docker and local providers already do.

chapters.title: Recording what the agent did
chapters.summary: An append-only journal of every frame, and a projection that never guesses.
chapters.takeaway: PyRIT records what the agent **did**, not only what it **said**. The journal is the ground truth; the projection into memory pieces is explicit, provenance-carrying, and silent about anything it cannot establish.

steps.title: Journal → pieces
steps.takeaway: The faithfulness of tool records is the review that deserves undivided attention. A false `function_call_output` is **false evidence**. This chapter is why PR 2c is its own PR.

steps.title: Every frame, both directions, plus lifecycle and inference
steps.body: Directions are `outgoing`, `incoming`, `lifecycle`, `stderr` and `inference`. Writes are appended under a lock after redaction of every credential value the execution knows about, including the relay token. The page API reads by sequence, so a browser can resume exactly where it left off.

captions.label: fixture
captions.text: These six are sequences 7–12 of a real capture made with the scripted ACP agent in this repository.

steps.title: Project explicit calls; never infer from claims
steps.body: The projector walks one turn's events in order and keeps a call only when the agent **named** the tool, reported **object** arguments, was **granted** permission (or never needed it), and both invocation and result are **established** by frames. Prose like “I ran the tests” is not a tool call.

captions.label: input
captions.text: Events of exactly one execution turn, strictly ordered; anything else is a `ValueError`.

focus: without guessing tool names or invocation from claims

steps.title: Four conditions, each visible as a slot
steps.body: Each condition is checked from frames, not from the model's text. When all four hold, two pieces are emitted. When any fails, the call is **omitted** and the reason is kept on the projection, so a reviewer can tell “no tools” from “tools we could not trust”.

captions.label: ambiguity
captions.text: Two call reports with the same id and different names → `ambiguous_call_reports`.

steps.title: Provenance travels with the piece
steps.body: Each emitted piece carries `agent_tool_call` metadata: the source protocol, execution id, turn id, the agent's own call id and the **event sequence** it was established from. From any score you can open the exact journal frame.

captions.label: call id
captions.text: `<execution>:<turn>:<agent call id>` so ids never collide across executions.

steps.title: Silence is explicit too
steps.body: The projection has an `omitted` map keyed by the agent's call id with one of the five reasons. `AgentTarget` puts the projection summary on the response metadata, so a scorer or a human can see that something was attempted but not established.

captions.label: deny by default
captions.text: With the default `deny` policy, a Copilot `tool_call` that asked permission shows up here, not as a result.

steps.title: Scorers already read this
steps.body: `MessageToolCallScorer` and friends consume `function_call` pieces today. Co-PyRIT's auto-scoring picks the pieces that are **scorable**: assistant or tool role, not a request trace, and a `completed` outcome. No new scorer type was needed.

captions.label: terminology
captions.text: “Tool calls”, matching the piece types; not “evidence”, which upstream now uses for findings.

chapters.title: Bring your own model, keep your own key
chapters.summary: The harness thinks it is talking to OpenAI. It is talking to a lease-scoped relay in front of a PyRIT target.
chapters.takeaway: The model behind the agent is **a PyRIT target**. The harness receives an execution-scoped token and a local base URL; the relay validates every request against the binding and forwards it with the single-inference capability. The provider credential stays on the server. Model and harness become **independently testable**.

steps.title: Bring your own model
steps.takeaway: An agent is a harness **and** a model. To test either one you must be able to hold the other fixed. PR 4 makes the model a PyRIT target behind a relay, which is also how no provider credential ever enters an environment.

steps.title: The harness is configured, not modified
steps.body: Each harness adapter knows how its harness selects a provider. For Copilot CLI that is `COPILOT_PROVIDER_BASE_URL`, `_TYPE=openai`, `_WIRE_API`, `_API_KEY` and `COPILOT_MODEL`; for the Agent Framework host it is the `OPENAI_*` family. The values are the relay URL translated by the environment and the lease token.

captions.label: reserved
captions.text: Those variable names are **reserved**: a profile cannot set them, so a template cannot point the harness elsewhere.

steps.title: A lease, not a key
steps.body: The relay hashes the bearer value and looks up an **active lease**. No lease → 401. Over budget or more than four concurrent requests → 429. The token is also added to the execution's redaction set, so it never appears in the journal in clear.

captions.label: revocation
captions.text: `revoke_async` cancels in-flight tasks when the execution closes or is cancelled.

steps.title: The body is policed against the binding
steps.body: Path must match the bound wire API; `model` must equal the binding; routing and auth overrides are refused; server-side continuation is refused; tools must be harness-executed function declarations; provider file references are refused. The harness gets exactly the model it was bound to, nothing adjacent.

slots.relay.check: path ✓ · model ✓ · no overrides ✓ · no continuation ✓ · tools: function only

captions.label: why so strict
captions.text: A compromised or merely creative harness must not be able to use PyRIT's credential as a general proxy.

focus: Model does not match this execution binding

steps.limit: Per-request modality enforcement (rejecting undeclared `image_url` / `input_image` parts) is deferred; the binding declares input modalities.

steps.title: Forwarded to a PyRIT target with the single-inference capability
steps.body: PR 3 gives targets a **single-inference** capability: transport and auth without history or a tool loop. The relay uses it, streaming the provider's response back to the harness. The binding records the target's identifier hash and protocol on the execution, so a result always knows which model answered.

captions.label: blocked
captions.text: A harness profile that names a provider credential is refused by BYOK (`native_model_credentials`).

steps.title: Captured both ways, bounded and redacted
steps.body: Every relayed request is journaled as `inference.started` → `inference.response` → `inference.finished` with byte counts and outcome. Content capture is **optional**; when on, decoded response text is journaled after the stream settles so a credential spanning transport chunks is redacted as a whole.

captions.label: correlation
captions.text: `turn_correlation: active_execution_turn_window`: inference events are attributed to the turn in flight.

steps.title: Model and harness, tested independently
steps.body: Hold the harness and swap the bound target: is the regression in the model? Hold the model and swap the harness (Copilot CLI, an Agent Framework agent, any ACP agent): is it in the scaffolding? Both are one configuration change, and the binding appears in every result's identity.

slots.binding.target: swap here → same harness, different model

captions.label: native credentials
captions.text: A harness may still use its own login (e.g. `COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN`) when no model is bound; then PyRIT records that no binding exists.

chapters.title: A target is a recipe, not a resource
chapters.summary: Model binding + harness profile + environment template → a configured target whose identity is the hash of the recipe.
chapters.takeaway: A configured `AgentTarget` **owns no resources**. Its identity is its configuration without defaults, timeouts and evidence budgets. Preset names are **provenance**, not identity. `permission_policy` **is** identity, and it defaults to deny.

steps.title: Recipes and identity
steps.takeaway: Operators compose agents from three reusable parts. PyRIT must know when two results came from the **same** system under test, so identity has to be exact: no names, no timeouts, no defaults.

steps.title: Three parts, one recipe
steps.body: **Model binding**: which registered PyRIT target answers inference, over which wire API. **Harness profile**: which agent kind, its command and declared credentials. **Environment template**: which provider, which image or workspace base, which network. Each is reusable and registered by setup, never fetched from the UI as import strings.

captions.label: composition
captions.text: `AgentTargetComposition` is frozen and `extra=forbid`; references are resolved before the target exists.

steps.title: Identity is the hash of the recipe
steps.body: `AgentTarget` builds its identifier from the configuration serialised without defaults and without the fields that are **execution policy rather than identity**: timeouts, holds, evidence and artifact budgets. Two operators who compose the same recipe from different preset names get the same identity.

captions.label: environment
captions.text: `environment` has no default: a target must say where it runs.

focus: Timeouts and evidence budgets are execution policy

steps.title: Permission policy is identity, and it defaults to deny
steps.body: A target that **asks an operator** and one that **denies** every tool permission are different systems under test, so `permission_policy` is hashed. New targets, in Python and in the UI, refuse permission requests. `allow_once` and `ask` are explicit choices; `ask` is only valid for interactive Co-PyRIT sends and fails fast for attacks.

captions.label: not enforcement
captions.text: The policy is a deterministic ACP permission response; the environment is the enforcement boundary.

steps.title: Names are provenance, not identity
steps.body: `AgentTargetInitializer` composes registered model, harness and environment presets into one named target from YAML. The names and origin are kept on the catalog entry as `agent_configuration_provenance` so a reviewer can see **how** a target was built, while identity stays the resolved recipe.

captions.label: deferred
captions.text: A Registry tab to browse presets, and “create by preset name” over REST, are deferred; the three-panel Create Target form stays the primary path.

focus: Compose registered model, harness, and environment settings

steps.title: Admin-only over REST; fixtures confined
steps.body: Every execution launches a process or container with credentials the server holds, regardless of parameters, so creating an `AgentTarget` through the API is **administrator-only** via `requires_admin_creation`. `agent_configuration` arrives as one validated object through the `JsonParameterValue` opt-in (exactly one parameter in the repository). Fixture directories reuse upstream's `upload_directory_parameter` confinement.

captions.label: replacement
captions.text: Live executions, including idle and held chats, block configuration replacement, exactly as active sends do.

chapters.title: Watch it, approve it, hold it
chapters.summary: Live streaming of durable evidence; permission requests routed to an operator; hold, cancel and close.
chapters.takeaway: Observation and control are separate PRs because they are separate concerns. 6a/6b let an operator **watch** what the agent does, live, from the journal. PR 7 lets the operator **change** what happens: approve or deny a tool, hold an execution, cancel, close.

steps.title: Operators in the loop
steps.takeaway: An agent that can act needs a person who can say no. Chapter 06 shows how Co-PyRIT streams the journal to the browser, and how a permission request travels from the harness to an operator and back, **as a denial when denied**, never as a cancellation.

steps.title: Watch what it does, live, from the journal
steps.body: The conversation stream is Server-Sent Events over the execution's durable journal: `state` snapshots, `events` pages by sequence, `reset` when a new execution replaces an old one, and `reconnect` when authorization must be refreshed. Nothing is held only in memory; a browser can reconnect and catch up by sequence.

slots.api.rev: transcript_revision bumps on every projected piece

captions.label: per conversation
captions.text: The store notifies subscribers per conversation id, so one chat's events do not wake every tab.

steps.title: The agent asks; the execution is held
steps.body: With `permission_policy=ask`, an ACP `session/request_permission` becomes an **approval** owned by the runtime. The harness must have offered a `reject_once` option, otherwise the request is invalid: a denial must be expressible as a denial. The execution enters `held` with a deadline.

captions.label: attacks
captions.text: `ask` is only valid for interactive sends; attacks with `ask` fail fast instead of hanging on a prompt nobody will answer.

steps.title: An operator decides
steps.body: The browser posts a decision. `AgentApprovals.decide_async` accepts exactly four decisions: `operator_allow`, `operator_deny`, `timeout_deny`, `cancelled`. It resolves the pending future with the matching ACP option (`allow_once` or `reject_once`) and journals `permission.resolved` with the actor.

captions.label: commit point
captions.text: The journal write is the commit point; a stale execution snapshot cannot reverse a decision.

steps.title: A denial is a denial, not a cancellation
steps.body: If nobody answers before the deadline, the approval settles as `timeout_deny` by **policy**; if the execution is cancelled, pending approvals settle as `cancelled` by the **runtime**. Each is told to the harness through the protocol option it offered, so the agent's own account of what happened stays truthful.

slots.approvals.timeout: deadline pauses while the hold is extended

captions.label: projection
captions.text: A denied call never becomes a `function_call_output`; it is omitted as `permission_not_granted`.

steps.title: Hold, cancel, close
steps.body: Execution states are explicit: `starting · idle · working · held · closing · closed · cleanup_failed`. An operator can extend a hold, cancel the current turn (ACP `session/cancel` with a grace period), or close the execution; administrators close anyone's from Registry → Agent executions. `cleanup_failed` is a state, not a log line.

captions.label: replacement
captions.text: An idle or held execution still blocks configuration replacement; it is a live resource.

steps.title: Who decided is visible, by default
steps.body: Decisions name the operator who made them to everyone with access to the attack. With `show_agent_operator_identity: false` the routes report roles instead (`operator`), while runtime actors (`policy`, `runtime`) are always shown as themselves. The journal keeps the real actor either way.

captions.label: setting
captions.text: Loader + app-state setting; default **show**.

chapters.title: Copilot CLI, Agent Framework, any ACP agent
chapters.summary: One adapter contract; Copilot CLI first, an in-repo ACP host for Agent Framework agents, and a login-free CI proof.
chapters.takeaway: `HarnessAdapter` is the second seam: how a harness is **launched** and how it is **pointed at a model**. Copilot CLI is the MVP harness. The optional Agent Framework host makes PyRIT itself an ACP agent for Microsoft Agent Framework agents, and doubles as the CI proof of the full ACP path without any login.

actors.label: CI proof
actors.sub: scripted ACP agent + Agent Framework agent through the relay

actors.label: verify_harness_adapter
actors.sub: reserved names, credential rules, environment translation

steps.title: Harnesses
steps.takeaway: The agent under test is whatever speaks ACP on stdio. PyRIT ships adapters for the harness it targets first, Copilot CLI, and for its own host of Microsoft Agent Framework agents; everything else is the generic adapter.

steps.title: One adapter contract
steps.body: An adapter declares `info` (name, default command, supported wire APIs, native credential names, reserved variables), `launch_environment` (how the harness finds its private home) and `inference_environment` (how it is pointed at the relay). Process identity and lookup paths are reserved for the execution and can never be credential references.

captions.label: registry
captions.text: `HarnessAdapterRegistry` is setup-owned; profiles reference adapters by name.

steps.title: Copilot CLI over ACP
steps.body: `copilot --acp --stdio`. Native credentials (`COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN`, `GH_TOKEN`, `GITHUB_TOKEN`) may be passed when no model is bound; with a binding, BYOK refuses them and the Copilot provider variables are reserved so nothing can redirect the harness.

captions.label: verified
captions.text: Integration-tested locally and in Docker with BYOK through the relay.

steps.title: Agent Framework: PyRIT's own ACP host
steps.body: An optional extra. `pyrit.agent.hosts.agent_framework_acp` wraps any Agent Framework agent as an ACP agent: it owns the agent and its tools inside the environment, emits `tool_call` / `tool_call_update` with **declared** tool names, and reports `cancelled` only for a real ACP `session/cancel`. The model side is the `OPENAI_*` family, so the relay works unchanged.

captions.label: declined review item
captions.text: The host imports `pyrit.models` inside the tested process by design; lazy package inits keep that to a pydantic model import.

steps.title: The seam is executable; CI proves the path
steps.body: `verify_harness_adapter` checks an adapter's promises the same way the environment suite checks a provider. Integration tests run a scripted ACP agent and an Agent Framework agent through the relay with **no login**, so the full path (ACP, journal, projection, relay, approvals) is proven on every CI run.

captions.label: fixtures in this deck
captions.text: Chapters 01 and 03 use a journal and projection captured from that scripted agent.

chapters.eyebrow: Deep dive · decisions a reviewer should know about
chapters.title: Nine decisions, each with its line of code
chapters.summary: Hover a decision for the rationale and the exact lines that implement it.

steps.title: Nine decisions

nodes.label: Admin gating
nodes.title: Admin-only over REST
nodes.claim: **Admin-only over REST.** Every execution launches a process or container with credentials the server holds, regardless of parameters, so `requires_admin_creation` is enforced next to upstream's `code_execution_parameter` and `server_credential_parameter`.

nodes.label: External input
nodes.title: One opt-in object over REST
nodes.claim: **One opt-in object over REST.** Upstream's allowlist admits scalars, lists and registry references. `agent_configuration` is a single-shape pydantic model, so a sibling opt-in, `JsonParameterValue`, lets exactly one parameter arrive as an object; the 35 other model-typed parameters stay in-process and a negative test locks that in.

nodes.label: Terminology
nodes.title: “Tool calls”, not “evidence”
nodes.claim: **“Tool calls”, not “evidence”.** Matches `MessageToolCallScorer` and the `function_call` piece types; upstream now uses “evidence” for findings.

nodes.label: Ownership
nodes.title: Policy in core, resources outside
nodes.claim: **Policy in core, resources outside.** Timeouts, budgets, cancellation, approvals, redaction and ACP live in core; allocation, release, seeding and byte streams live in providers; adapters own launch and environment translation.

nodes.label: Identity
nodes.title: Hash of the recipe, minus policy
nodes.claim: **Hash of the recipe, minus policy.** `environment` is required; Docker-typed fields are validated by the Docker provider; `permission_policy` **is** identity.

nodes.label: Deny default
nodes.title: Permissions default to deny
nodes.claim: **Permissions default to deny.** `allow_once` and `ask` are explicit; `ask` only for interactive sends; a harness must offer `reject_once` before `ask` asks anyone, so a denial is never reported as a cancellation.

nodes.label: Confined fixtures
nodes.title: Fixture dirs confined over REST
nodes.claim: **Fixture dirs confined over REST.** API-created targets reuse upstream's `upload_directory_parameter` contract; Python callers are not confined.

nodes.label: Operator identity
nodes.title: Operator identity shown by default
nodes.claim: **Operator identity shown by default.** Decisions name the operator to everyone with access to the attack; `show_agent_operator_identity: false` reports roles. Presentation only.

nodes.claim: **Bounded, redacted capture.** Optional inference content capture journals decoded text after the stream settles so a credential spanning chunks is redacted whole; budgets default to 100 requests, cap 1,000; live executions block configuration replacement.

steps.footer: Two review observations were explicitly **declined**: the catalog shows credential variable **names** and the resolved fixture path to every authenticated user (documented as the authoring contract), and the Agent Framework host imports `pyrit.models` inside the tested process (lazy package inits keep that to a pydantic model import; the host is PyRIT code by design).
